demos.title: From a chat message to a pull request
demos.scenario: Maya's service needs a health check.
demos.payoff: A reviewed pull request, and no model key on Maya's laptop
demos.next: What would your team hand off next?
demos.intro: This demo follows Maya, a developer on the inventory team whose service has no health check. She asks her usual coding client for the change, the way she would ask a colleague. Orka runs the agents on her team's cluster and keeps the records. We'll check the resulting pull request on GitHub. The model key never reaches her laptop.

chapters.title: Connect with a cluster token
chapters.cue: Provider = the saved connection Orka uses to reach a model
chapters.text: The model key stays in a cluster Secret. A Provider holds the connection settings Orka uses to reach that model. The platform team also defined three Agents: a coder, a reviewer, and an analyst. Maya connects with a token for the cluster. The status check confirms Orka is ready. Short commands such as readme are shell helpers defined in this demo script.

chapters.title: Ask in the familiar client
chapters.cue: Claude Code sends its requests to Orka
chapters.text: Here is the service today, with no health check. Two environment variables point the coding client at Orka. Maya asks for the endpoint, a test, the docs, and a pull request. She does not choose which agents do the work. She sends it as an ordinary prompt.

chapters.marker: Orka turns the chat into Tasks
chapters.title: Watch the work happen
chapters.cue: Task = one piece of work, with a record
chapters.text: Each row is a Task, one piece of work Orka runs and keeps a record of. Orka decides how many to run and in what order, so more than one can run at once. A failed row shows an attempt that did not complete. We check the final result before calling the work complete. Waiting time is cut.

chapters.marker: Open the Task that made the pull request
chapters.title: Read the receipt
chapters.cue: Publisher = the one component that holds the Git token
chapters.text: We open the Task whose branch became the pull request and read what the coder said as it worked. The coder never pushed. Orka's Publisher, the one component that holds a Git token, verified the files and published the branch. Verified Exact means what reached GitHub is exactly what Orka checked.

chapters.title: Check it outside Orka
chapters.cue: Real pull request, passing checks, recorded changes
chapters.text: Maya's answer arrived in the chat window. Now we check GitHub itself: the pull request, its checks, and the changed files. The closing table comes from the records we queried: the message, the Tasks observed during the run, including failed attempts, and the pull request. Maya used a cluster token to access the model.

demos.outro: One chat message became a reviewed pull request, with records linking the completed work to the code on GitHub. What would you hand off to your own agent team? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for setup steps and more examples.

demos.title: A workspace that sleeps
demos.scenario: Add a health check today. Look at the same files tomorrow.
demos.payoff: Nothing runs in between, and nothing is lost
demos.next: What work would you come back to tomorrow?
demos.intro: This demo follows Maya on the inventory team as she asks an agent to add a health check today and returns to the same files tomorrow. Orka stops the agent's Pod between requests but keeps the workspace disk. We'll check what survives. The saved disk and cluster still have costs.

chapters.marker: The platform team chose the lifecycle
chapters.title: Choose how the workspace waits
chapters.cue: Workspace class = a lifecycle the platform team saved
chapters.text: A workspace class is a lifecycle the platform team saved once. Maya asks for it by name. This one says: when the agent stops, put its host to sleep and keep the disk. The host is the Kubernetes Agent Sandbox project. Before Maya's request, it is empty. Short commands such as request are shell helpers defined in this demo script.

chapters.title: Give the agent a place to work
chapters.cue: Session = a conversation Orka remembers
chapters.text: A Task is one request with a recorded outcome. It opens a Session, a conversation Orka remembers, and names the class and the repository. The host starts one Pod for the agent and one small disk. We check for four common model and Git credential variables without displaying any values. The agent adds the endpoint, and Orka's Publisher opens the pull request.

chapters.title: Stop the idle worker
chapters.cue: No Pod, only a disk
chapters.text: The agent is done and the Session is idle. The class said sleep, so Orka asks the host to suspend the Sandbox. The Pod goes away and the disk stays. The idle agent no longer reserves CPU or memory. The cluster and the saved disk still have costs.

chapters.title: Return to the same files
chapters.cue: Same Sandbox identity, new Pod, kept disk
chapters.text: The follow-up names the same Session. The host wakes the same Sandbox, with the same identity, and starts a new Pod on the kept disk. The agent finds yesterday's endpoint. The Task records that publication made no change.

chapters.title: Finish the workspace lifecycle
chapters.cue: The records and the pull request stay
chapters.text: Deleting the workspace removes the Sandbox and its disk. The Task records and the pull request stay. The closing table shows two requests, one Sandbox identity on both days, zero Pods while asleep, and the open pull request.

demos.outro: Two requests used one set of files, with the worker stopped in between. The platform team chose the lifecycle once, and Maya used it by name. What work would you come back to tomorrow? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for setup steps and more examples.

demos.title: A save point for an agent
demos.scenario: An audit must survive a pause and a deleted workspace.
demos.payoff: The audit comes back from a checkpoint
demos.next: Which work would you want a save point for?
demos.intro: This demo follows Priya on the security team as she audits the inventory service. She needs the agent to stop between requests and the audit files to survive deletion of the workspace. Orka keeps a checkpoint. We'll suspend the workspace, delete it, and compare the restored audit with the original.

chapters.marker: Substrate keeps a pool of workers
chapters.title: Meet the workspace host
chapters.cue: Actor = an isolated environment hosted by a shared worker
chapters.text: This host is Agent Substrate. It keeps a few worker Pods ready all the time and runs each agent inside an Actor, an isolated environment with its own kernel, hosted by whichever worker is free. The platform team's class says: sleep when the agent stops, keep the data, and boot a fresh Actor from it next time. Short commands such as actors are shell helpers defined in this demo script.

chapters.title: Write the audit
chapters.cue: Task = the request; Session = the conversation
chapters.text: The request is a Task. It opens a Session, names the class, and asks for at most six findings written to a file. Orka creates an Actor and Substrate places it on a worker. The agent writes the findings. Orka's Publisher, which alone holds the Git token, publishes them as a branch.

chapters.title: Keep the files, release the worker
chapters.cue: Zero Actors, every worker free
chapters.text: The agent is done. Substrate captures the Actor's data to storage, removes the Actor, and retires the worker that hosted it. The pool gets a clean replacement, so the next agent never inherits a used worker. Zero Actors are running and the audit's files are in storage.

chapters.title: Keep an independent save point
chapters.cue: Checkpoint = a copy of the data, with a digest
chapters.text: A checkpoint is a copy of the workspace's data that Orka keeps as an object of its own, with a digest. Priya creates one. It survives the workspace it came from being deleted.

chapters.marker: Delete the workspace, restore the copy
chapters.title: Restore after deleting the source
chapters.cue: A new Task restores from the checkpoint by identity and digest
chapters.text: Now the worst case. The workspace is deleted, and with it the data Substrate kept. A brand-new Task, outside the old Session, restores from the checkpoint by its identity and digest, so a swapped copy would be refused. The audit comes back line for line, and Orka publishes it again.

chapters.title: Check what is left
chapters.cue: Restored workspace and checkpoint removed; records kept
chapters.text: The restored Task finishes and its workspace is removed. We also delete the checkpoint. The final records show the remaining Actors and free workers, the checkpoint digest, the deleted original workspace, and matching audit files from both published commits.

demos.outro: The audit survived a pause and the deletion of its workspace, and came back from a save point. Substrate saved the files and started new Actors. Orka chose when, and kept the records. Which work would you want a save point for? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for setup steps and more examples.

demos.title: Findings that arrive as pull requests
demos.scenario: An old app needs a security review people can act on.
demos.payoff: A checked finding becomes a pull request Priya chose
demos.next: Which repository would you start with?
demos.intro: This demo follows Priya on the security team as she scans an old Node.js app. She wants findings checked before she reads them and fixes she can review as pull requests. We use a public test application with known vulnerabilities. Priya chooses which validated finding to patch.

chapters.title: Register once
chapters.cue: One record: the repository, a reviewing Agent, a patching Agent
chapters.text: Priya registers the repository once. The record names the repository, the Agent that reviews, and the Agent that patches. Only Orka's Publisher ever holds the Git credentials. The agents that read and patch the code never do. Registering starts the first scan. Short commands such as registration are shell helpers defined in this demo script.

chapters.title: Watch the review take shape
chapters.cue: Stages, with counts of Tasks by phase
chapters.text: The reviewing Agent first writes a threat model: what the app does and where an attacker would push. Then it reviews the code slice by slice against that model, and checks the likely findings. Each row is one stage of the scan with a count of its Tasks by phase. Waiting is cut. The scan ends with a threat model and findings on record.

chapters.title: Read one finding
chapters.cue: Listed findings passed validation; inspect the evidence
chapters.text: Every finding cites a file and a line. Orka then checks the two most severe likely findings in an isolated worker. The list includes only findings marked validated. We open one to see the affected code, its severity, and the evidence recorded with it.

chapters.title: Decide, then check GitHub
chapters.cue: A person picks; Orka opens the pull request
chapters.text: Nothing is patched by itself. Priya asks for a fix on this one finding. Orka hands it to the coding Agent in a writable workspace, and the Publisher opens the pull request with credentials the agent never saw. We check GitHub itself: the pull request is open and lists the changed files. The closing table counts the slices reviewed, the findings validated, and the fix Priya requested.

demos.outro: The scan produced checked findings, Priya chose one, and a pull request arrived for her team to review. Which repository would you start with? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for setup steps and more examples.

demos.title: Two teams, one URL
demos.scenario: Payments and inventory need different models and separate work.
demos.payoff: The caller's token picks the team, and the wrong door stays shut
demos.next: How would you organize your teams?
demos.intro: This demo follows Alice on the payments team and Bob on inventory as they use the same AI address. They need different models and budgets, and each team's work must stay separate. Each team has its own Orka. A router uses the caller's token to pick the team. We'll check the routing and two refused cross-team requests.

chapters.title: Give each team its own installation
chapters.cue: Namespace = a team's own room in the cluster
chapters.text: Each team has its own namespace, a room of its own in the cluster, with a complete Orka inside: its own model key, Agents, and Tasks. In front of both sits one small router. It reads the caller's token and forwards to that team. It holds no keys and runs no models. Short commands such as routes are shell helpers defined in this demo script.

chapters.marker: Alice and Bob use the same URL
chapters.title: Connect two people to one address
chapters.cue: Same URL, different tokens
chapters.text: The token is the badge. It says who you are and which room you belong to, and it goes where an API key normally goes. Asking the same URL which models it offers gives Alice the payments models and Bob the inventory models. The token chose the team. Nothing in the request did.

chapters.marker: The same request lands in different homes
chapters.title: See where the work runs
chapters.cue: Task = the record of work, inside the caller's team
chapters.text: Both ask the coding client for the same small thing. Each request becomes a Task in its own team's installation, run by that team's Orka on that team's budget, and nowhere else.

chapters.marker: Bob knocks on the wrong door
chapters.title: Try the wrong team's resources
chapters.cue: Wrong model and wrong namespace refused
chapters.text: Bob asks for the payments team's model through the shared URL. The request reaches inventory and is refused because that installation does not offer the model. Bob then goes straight to payments with his token. Refused again. Each installation checks identity. The closing table shows one URL, two installations, and both refusals.

demos.outro: One address serves separate teams without putting their work in the same installation. Each team keeps its own models, budget, and records. How would you organize your teams? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for setup steps and more examples.

demos.title: The order desk asks for help
demos.scenario: A customer wants 24 filters. Only 18 are available today.
demos.payoff: A reply Sam's app can retry, continue, and read back
demos.next: Which application could ask your agents for help?
demos.intro: This demo follows Sam, who runs the order desk, as a customer asks for twenty four replacement filters. Only eighteen are in stock, and the customer needs them today. Sam's application asks the inventory team's agent for advice. That agent runs in Orka. We'll send the request, retry it, and continue the conversation.

chapters.title: Start with the customer
chapters.cue: 24 requested, 18 available, delivery tomorrow
chapters.text: Here is the whole request: the stock, the delivery, and what Sam needs. The application supplies those facts and asks for a recommendation. Short commands such as card are shell helpers defined in this demo script.

chapters.title: Discover what the agent can do
chapters.cue: Agent Card = what an agent does and how to reach it
chapters.text: Sam's app and Orka speak A2A, a common format for asking another agent for help. The inventory agent publishes a card with one skill: recommend a customer reply from the stock facts supplied.

chapters.marker: Send the work and get a receipt
chapters.title: Submit and keep the reference
chapters.cue: Task = Orka's record of one piece of work
chapters.text: The app gives the request a stable ID and asks for an immediate acknowledgement. It gets a reference and a conversation ID. Behind the reference is a Task, Orka's record of this piece of work. Sam's app can check on it with the reference alone.

chapters.title: Read the answer
chapters.cue: The same answer through A2A and in Orka's record
chapters.text: The answer arrives: offer eighteen today and six after tomorrow's delivery, with a short customer reply. It is the same through A2A and in Orka's own record, and it used the facts we supplied.

chapters.title: Retry safely
chapters.cue: Same ID, same Task, no duplicate work
chapters.text: Applications retry when they are unsure a request arrived. Sending the same request ID again returns the same reference and the same Task. A retry does not do the work twice.

chapters.title: Continue the conversation
chapters.cue: Session = the conversation shared by related Tasks
chapters.text: A new request ID starts new work, and keeping the conversation ID connects it to the earlier exchange. Orka calls that shared conversation a Session. The follow-up knew what the first request said. The closing table shows three requests sent, one Task after the retry, and two Tasks in one Session.

demos.outro: Sam's app got a usable reply, retried safely, and continued the conversation, with every step on record in Orka. Which application could ask your agents for help? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for setup steps and more examples.

demos.title: Check stock, keep purchasing closed
demos.scenario: The assistant needs supplier information, without buying anything.
demos.payoff: Stock confirmed, zero orders created, both sides on record
demos.next: Which actions should your platform allow?
demos.intro: This demo follows Jordan from the inventory team, who needs twenty more replacement filters. An assistant can check stock, but the platform team has not allowed purchasing. We'll request both actions and check the supplier's own receipts to see what reached it. The supplier is a test service with made-up stock.

chapters.title: Ask for information first
chapters.cue: The supplier starts with zero orders
chapters.text: Here is the request. The supplier is a small service with made-up stock, and its receipts are the proof. Before we start, it has created zero orders. Short commands such as tool are shell helpers defined in this demo script.

chapters.marker: 2. The assistant can request two actions
chapters.title: Define what the model can ask for
chapters.cue: Tool = an action the model can ask Orka to carry out
chapters.text: A Tool is an action the model can ask Orka to carry out. This assistant has two: check stock and place an order. Both go through a gateway. Neither Tool contains the supplier credential. A Secret holds it, and the gateway supplies it.

chapters.marker: 3. The gateway allows one of them
chapters.title: Read the one route
chapters.cue: Stock lookups pass; nothing is configured for orders
chapters.text: The gateway forwards only what its routes allow, and there is one route: the stock lookup. Nothing is configured for orders.

chapters.title: Run the allowed lookup
chapters.cue: Task = the work record, with tool events and the result
chapters.text: A Task is Orka's record of one piece of work. The assistant calls the stock Tool, the call completes, and it answers that thirty-two filters are available. The supplier's own record shows the request arrived with the credential the model never saw.

chapters.title: Attempt the closed action
chapters.cue: Refused at the gateway; zero orders at the supplier
chapters.text: Now we explicitly ask the assistant to place the order. Asking for an action does not grant permission to perform it. The gateway had no route for the order and refused it. The assistant reports that no order was placed, and the supplier still counts zero orders. The closing table shows both requests from both sides.

demos.outro: The assistant got the stock information it needed while purchasing stayed closed. The platform controlled the route and the credential, and the supplier's receipts agree. Which actions should your platform allow? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for setup steps and more examples.

demos.title: A procedure the next agent can use
demos.scenario: Keep a return procedure, with a person deciding what is shared.
demos.payoff: A fresh agent answers from the reviewed note, with the trail on record
demos.next: Which team knowledge is worth keeping?
demos.intro: This demo follows Jordan, who runs the warehouse, as a return procedure becomes shared knowledge. An assistant has just read the procedure for replacement filters, and the next assistant needs it too. Orka lets the first agent propose a note. Jordan reviews it, then explicitly publishes it before a fresh agent can use it.

chapters.title: Start with the source note
chapters.cue: Memory = saved team knowledge Orka hands to future work
chapters.text: Returned filters go to Dock Three with a particular return label. Memory here means saved team knowledge Orka hands to future work. Right now there are no shared notes. Short commands such as notes are shell helpers defined in this demo script.

chapters.title: Let the agent suggest what to keep
chapters.cue: remember proposes a note; apply publishes it
chapters.text: A Task is Orka's record of one piece of work. This one asks an assistant to propose the reusable part of the procedure. The remember tool files a proposal for a person, with the text and the Task it came from. Nothing is shared yet.

chapters.marker: 3. A fresh agent does not know it yet
chapters.title: Try the question before publication
chapters.cue: No tools, no shared conversation
chapters.text: A different assistant gets only the question, in a new Task, with no conversation history. It says the procedure is unavailable. It did not guess, and the records show it called no tools.

chapters.title: Record the decision, then publish
chapters.cue: Accept records the decision; apply publishes the note
chapters.text: Jordan checks the proposal against the operations note and accepts it. Accepting records the decision, and the count of shared notes is still zero. Publishing is a second, explicit step. After it, there is one shared note, and it still names the proposal it came from.

chapters.marker: 5. A fresh agent knows it now
chapters.title: Ask a new reader the same question
chapters.cue: Dock 3 and the label, from the reviewed note alone
chapters.text: Same reader, same question, another new Task, with no note and no history passed in. It answers Dock Three and the right label, with no tools and no shared conversation. The closing table links the original Task, the proposal, Jordan's review, the shared note, and the later Task.

demos.outro: One agent proposed a procedure, Jordan reviewed and published it, and a later agent used it, with a record linking the knowledge to its source. Which team knowledge is worth keeping? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for setup steps and more examples.

demos.title: Fibey investigates, a person approves
demos.scenario: A pressure reading changed after maintenance. Inspect before acting.
demos.payoff: One approved inspection, one work order, one Task
demos.next: Where should your agents pause for a decision?
demos.intro: This demo follows Fibey, an AI assistant, as it investigates a pump's pressure reading that dropped after maintenance. The other readings look normal. Creating a work order needs approval from Lee, the shift lead. Orka holds that action until Lee decides. The incident and the work-order service are simulated.

chapters.title: Read the incident before acting
chapters.cue: One reading disagrees with the rest
chapters.text: One pressure sensor fell while the second gauge, flow, and vibration stayed normal. The transmitter was replaced during maintenance and has not been checked. Worth a look before touching anything. Short commands such as counts are shell helpers defined in this demo script.

chapters.marker: 2. Fibey may look, but not act alone
chapters.title: Set the boundary
chapters.cue: Tool = an action Fibey can ask Orka to carry out
chapters.text: A Tool is an action Fibey can ask Orka to carry out. The platform team's policy lets Fibey read inventory on its own. Creating a work order needs a person. Before we start, the work-order service counts zero orders.

chapters.title: Start one Task
chapters.cue: Task = the request and its continuing record
chapters.text: One Task holds the whole thing: the investigation, the wait for a decision, and the result that comes back. Fibey reads the alert, checks inventory, and proposes a work order. Then it pauses inside the same Task.

chapters.title: Inspect what is waiting
chapters.cue: One inventory read, zero work orders
chapters.text: This is the exact action waiting for a decision: the pump, the summary, and a status of pending. The service counts one inventory lookup and zero work orders. Fibey asking did not authorize anything.

chapters.title: Approve, with a reason
chapters.cue: The decision records who, what, and why
chapters.text: Lee reads the proposal and approves the inspection, with a reason. The decision is on record: who approved, what, and why. Orka may now run the stored action.

chapters.marker: 6. The work order comes back to the same Task
chapters.title: Read the receipt and the answer
chapters.cue: Exactly one work order after the decision
chapters.text: The work order is created after the decision, and its receipt returns to Fibey inside the same Task. Fibey's answer names the work order and the next step. The closing table shows one lookup, zero orders before approval, one after, and the original Task retained.

demos.outro: Fibey investigated and proposed. Lee approved, and the receipt came back to the same waiting Task. Where should your agents pause for a decision? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for setup steps and more examples.

demos.title: Twenty customers, one checkout problem
demos.scenario: Twenty customer reports trace to one checkout retry bug.
demos.payoff: Same checked outcomes, measured time and estimated cost
demos.next: What would you measure for your team?
demos.intro: This demo follows Dana's platform team as it handles twenty customer reports of double charges after a frozen checkout. Support needs twenty replies and engineering needs one fix. The team runs the work twice, first on a hosted model, then with a router that can choose a small local model for support. Both runs face the same checks. We'll compare elapsed time and estimated cost.

chapters.title: Two Agents, two jobs
chapters.cue: Agent = saved instructions for an assistant
chapters.text: An Agent holds the instructions for an assistant. Support must write two factual sentences per customer, using the order reference when it is supplied and asking for it when it is missing. Engineering must fix the payment retry bug in the sample repository and pass its six tests. Short commands such as run batch are shell helpers defined in this demo script.

chapters.marker: 2. Run everything on the hosted model
chapters.title: Set the baseline
chapters.cue: Task = one piece of work; twenty replies plus one fix
chapters.text: A Task is Orka's record of one piece of work. Twenty support Tasks run one at a time, then one engineering Task, all on the hosted model. Waiting is cut. Every reply is checked against its customer message. The engineering agent reports its tests pass, and we check that ourselves in a sealed container. Twenty replies and six tests: that is the baseline.

chapters.marker: 3. Add a small model on our own hardware
chapters.title: Use hardware we already operate
chapters.cue: A small model on the cluster's CPUs
chapters.text: AIKit serves Qwen three point five, a small two-billion-parameter model, on the cluster's CPUs. It runs on hardware the team already pays for and operates. The table includes allocated CPU and memory during the measured windows, including idle time. It shows test preparation separately.

chapters.marker: 4. Let a router choose the model
chapters.title: Turn routing on
chapters.cue: Provider = Orka's connection to a model service
chapters.text: A Provider is Orka's connection to a model service. Support's Provider, named semantic router, points at Vekil. Vekil has a semantic router: Jev, a classifier model, assesses new work and recommends lightweight or powerful. Our configuration maps that choice to local Qwen or the hosted model. If Jev is unavailable, Vekil uses the powerful model. Related tool calls keep the chosen model while the agent finishes its job. The Agents and requests are unchanged.

chapters.title: Repeat the work
chapters.cue: Same reports, same instructions, same starting code
chapters.text: The same twenty reports and engineering request run again, with the same checks. Thirteen replies used the local model. Seven fell back to hosted when Jev was unavailable. Engineering used five hosted calls, compared with eight before. In this run, it took seventy seven seconds instead of one hundred five, twenty six point seven percent less time. Both coding runs used the same hosted model. All twenty replies passed, and we independently reran the six payment tests.

chapters.title: Compare outcomes, time, and cost
chapters.cue: Service estimate: 46.6% lower  |  Support time: 68.0% longer
chapters.text: Using the dated rate card, estimated API charges went from about twenty nine cents to fifteen cents, down forty nine point one percent. Adding the stated share of hardware, the service estimate fell from about twenty nine cents to sixteen cents, down forty six point six percent. Support took two hundred sixty nine seconds, then four hundred fifty two, sixty eight percent longer. The hosted-only service estimate excludes local-model test preparation; the actual test totals below retain it. These are estimates, not an invoice. The seven failed classifier calls have zero-charge receipts, but their token counts are unavailable. Coding token counts are unavailable in Orka's report, so we use gateway records.

demos.outro: Both runs met the same checks. The routing-enabled run had a lower estimated cost, but support took longer. Orka defined the jobs and kept the records. Vekil chose the models, and AIKit supplied the local option. That lets the platform team change how work runs and measure the result. What would you tune for your team? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for setup steps and more examples.
